analysis.one_liner: Phases out fossil fuels to reach 100% clean and renewable energy, with aid for workers and low-income families.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 35 House Democrats, never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a national goal of 100% clean and renewable energy by 2050. It would cap the share of electricity from fossil fuels each year until it reaches zero, end a long list of tax breaks for oil, gas, and coal companies, and put a carbon fee on aviation, shipping, and rail. The money raised would fund a Climate Fund that pays for solar panels, home weatherization, energy bills, and electric public transit for low-income families, plus up to five years of wage, health, pension, and retraining benefits for workers who lose fossil fuel jobs. It also includes measures making it easier for workers to form unions at new clean energy projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income families get help paying for solar, home efficiency upgrades, and heating bills; fossil fuel workers get extended unemployment, health coverage, pensions, and free retraining; workers on federally funded construction get apprenticeship and local-hiring requirements; and clean energy, storage, and electric transit industries get grants and permanent tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income families and fossil fuel workers

how_it_helps.text: Grants and loans would pay the upfront cost of solar for households earning 80% or less of area median income, and community solar would reserve at least 25% of its power for low-income and disadvantaged households.
The bill would raise funding for low-income home energy assistance and weatherization out of the Climate Fund, and spend up to $30 billion a year on affordable zero-emission public transportation.

Workers laid off from coal and other fossil fuel jobs would qualify for federally funded unemployment checks (up to 156 weeks), health premium subsidies, pension top-ups, and up to four years of paid education or training.
Contractors on federally funded projects would have to fund preapprenticeship programs and aim for 30% of work hours by local, low-income, or disadvantaged workers.
Permanent, refundable tax credits for electric vehicles, energy-efficient homes, and renewable power would lower energy costs for households and businesses.
A Workplace Democracy Act subtitle would speed up union certification elections and require employers to bargain a first contract, covering workers on new clean energy projects.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies lose tax subsidies worth billions, face an annual cap on their share of electricity that reaches zero by 2050, and a moratorium on new major fossil fuel projects; airlines, shipping, and railroads pay a new carbon fee; the federal debt bears the cost of climate bonds funding the roughly $100-plus billion a year in programs; energy consumers could see higher prices if clean alternatives and storage lag behind the phaseout.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and bond-funded federal spending

drawbacks.text: The bill funds its grant programs by issuing climate bonds, adding federal borrowing on top of the roughly $76 billion in annual program caps named in the text ($30B transit, $10B solar, $10B weatherization, $24B energy assistance, and more).
The carbon fee on aviation, shipping, and rail would be passed on to shippers and travelers as higher freight and ticket costs.

Hard annual caps on fossil electricity with a fixed 2050 end date could strain the grid and raise electricity prices if energy storage and transmission build out more slowly than the phaseout requires.
Even with generous transition benefits, communities whose economies rest on coal and oil production would face concentrated job and tax-base losses that retraining money cannot fully replace.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is deliberately designed to spread the gains widely — helping the households that spend the largest share of income on energy, and compensating rather than abandoning the workers whose jobs it would phase out — but it does so with an enormous, debt-financed spending program and a rigid statutory phaseout whose feasibility depends on storage technology that did not exist at scale when it was written. The costs fall heavily on a single, politically powerful industry, which is exactly why it drew no Republican support and no floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2017 and referred to ten House committees, and then to eight subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it and it never reached the House floor before that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Polis introduced the 100 by '50 Act on July 19, 2017, joined by Reps. Grijalva, Huffman, and Jayapal as original cosponsors.

The Speaker referred the bill to ten committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Education and the Workforce, Financial Services, Natural Resources, Appropriations, Agriculture, Small Business, and Science, Space, and Technology — meaning each could claim part of it and no single panel had to act.
Over the following months, parts of the bill were further referred to eight subcommittees covering aviation, energy, water, highways, rail, commodity exchanges, and economic development.
The bill attracted 35 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, in a House where Republicans held the majority.
After the subcommittee referrals in May 2018, the bill saw no further action of any kind before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies came out ahead: they kept their tax subsidies, faced no cap on their share of the electricity market, and no carbon fee was imposed on transportation fuels, while low-income households got none of the bill's solar, weatherization, or bill assistance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies kept subsidies and faced no phaseout

for.name: Rep. Jared Polis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled its cosponsor list.

for.name: 35 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Speaker Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote, and referred it to ten committees where it stayed without action.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill was referred by the Republican-controlled House without ever being scheduled for a vote; no Republican supported it on the record.

industries.note: The bill terminates more than a dozen fossil fuel tax breaks (percentage depletion, LIFO accounting, the domestic manufacturing deduction, royalty capital gains treatment, and more), caps the share of electricity they can supply each year until it reaches zero in 2050, and bars new major fossil fuel projects. Their losses come directly as reduced subsidies and a shrinking market.

A new carbon fee would apply to aviation, maritime, and rail fossil fuel use to push those sectors toward zero emissions, raising their operating costs, which they would pass to travelers and shippers.

industries.industry: Renewable energy, energy storage, and electric vehicle makers
industries.note: The bill provides grants for energy storage and zero-emission heating, permanent tax credits for solar and wind facilities, EVs, and hybrid trucks, and large public transit and highway decarbonization programs — creating customers and guaranteed demand. It would also entrench them as the permanent suppliers of a public good, since federal energy assistance flows through the clean energy market the bill builds.

Utilities lose their fossil generation capacity on a statutory schedule but gain renewable tax credits and grid reliability and storage programs; low-income rate assistance funded through the Climate Fund reduces their bad-debt and shut-off costs.

A Workplace Democracy Act subtitle streamlines union certification and first-contract bargaining, and contractors on federally funded clean energy projects must run registered apprenticeships with targeted-hire goals, expanding union-represented work.
